chapter.chapter_subtitle: Type I, Type II, Type III, Mixed Conditionals, and Other Conditional Words — A Complete Student Guide
chapter.chapter_introduction: Welcome to Chapter 4 of Communicative English Language Skills I. Conditional sentences are one of the most important and frequently tested grammar structures in English. They are used to talk about possibilities, hypothetical situations, and their consequences. This chapter explains Type I, Type II, and Type III conditionals in full detail, along with mixed conditionals, other conditional words (unless, provided that, as long as, in case), and common errors. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to use conditional sentences confidently and correctly in your academic writing and daily communication.

sections.section_introduction: Before we examine each type of conditional, let us understand what a conditional sentence is and how it is structured.

subsections.subtitle: 4.1.1. Definition and Structure
paragraphs: A **conditional sentence** is a sentence that expresses a condition and its result. It has two parts: the **if-clause** (also called the conditional clause or protasis) and the **main clause** (also called the result clause or apodosis).
**Form:** If + condition, + result (or Result + if + condition)
**Example:** If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
- If-clause: If you study hard
- Main clause: you will pass the exam

**Oxford Reference (Murphy, English Grammar in Use, 4th ed.):** Conditional sentences are used to talk about a condition and its consequence. The if-clause describes the condition, and the main clause describes the result. The order of the clauses can be reversed without changing the meaning, but when the if-clause comes first, a comma is used.
**Example (reversed):** You will pass the exam if you study hard. (No comma when main clause comes first.)
**Key Idea:** Conditionals are used to talk about real possibilities, unreal or hypothetical situations, and impossible past situations.
definitions: A sentence that expresses a condition and its result.
The part of the sentence that expresses the condition (starts with 'if').
The part of the sentence that expresses the result.
key_points: Conditional sentence: condition + result.
Two parts: if-clause and main clause.
Order can be reversed.
Comma used when if-clause comes first.
Three main types: Type I, Type II, Type III.
formulas: Conditional Sentence
If + condition, + result
If you study, you will pass.
Reversed Order
Result + if + condition
You will pass if you study.

sections.section_introduction: Type I Conditional is used to talk about real or possible situations in the future. Let us explore its form, uses, and examples in detail.

subsections.subtitle: 4.2.1. Form and Structure
paragraphs: **Type I Conditional** (also called the First Conditional or Future Real Conditional) is used to talk about real or possible situations in the future. The condition is likely to happen, and the result is probable.
**Form:** If + present simple, + will + base verb
**Examples from the module:**
- 'If I don't finish it tonight, I will get an F!'
- 'I can help you if you need it.'
- 'We need to leave right now if we want to get there in time.'
- 'If you study hard, you will score A grade.'

**Oxford Reference (Murphy, English Grammar in Use, 4th ed.):** The first conditional is used for real possibilities. The if-clause uses the present simple (NOT 'will'), and the main clause uses 'will' + base verb. It is used to talk about what will happen if something happens.
**Important Note:** Do NOT use 'will' in the if-clause.
- Incorrect: If you will study hard, you will pass.
- Correct: If you study hard, you will pass.
**Variations:** The main clause can also use 'can', 'may', 'might', or the imperative.
- If you finish early, you can leave.
- If it rains, we may cancel the trip.
- If you see him, tell him to call me. (imperative)
definitions: A conditional used for real or possible situations in the future.
Another name for Type I Conditional.
Another name for Type I Conditional.
key_points: Type I: real/possible future situations.
Form: If + present simple, + will + base verb.
Do NOT use 'will' in the if-clause.
Main clause can use 'can', 'may', 'might', imperative.
Condition is likely; result is probable.
formulas: Type I Conditional
If + present simple, + will + base verb
If you study, you will pass.
Type I with Can
If + present simple, + can + base verb
If you finish, you can leave.
Type I with May/Might
If + present simple, + may/might + base verb
If it rains, we may cancel.
Type I with Imperative
If + present simple, + imperative
If you see him, tell him.

subsections.subtitle: 4.2.2. Uses and Examples
paragraphs: **Use 1: Real possibility in the future.**
- If I don't finish it tonight, I will get an F!
- If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
**Use 2: Offers and promises.**
- I can help you if you need it.
- If you finish early, you can leave.
**Use 3: Warnings and instructions.**
- If you see him, tell him to call me.
- If it rains, we may cancel the trip.
**More examples:**
- If you eat too much, you will feel sick.
- If she calls, I will let you know.
- If they arrive late, we will start without them.
- If you don't hurry, we will miss the bus.
definitions: A proposal to do something for someone.
A statement about a possible negative consequence.
key_points: Type I is used for real possibilities.
It can be used for offers, promises, warnings, and instructions.
The if-clause uses present simple.
The main clause uses 'will' + base verb.
Never use 'will' in the if-clause.
tables: If you study, you will pass.
I can help you if you need it.
If you don't hurry, we will miss the bus.
If you see him, tell him to call me.

sections.section_introduction: Type II Conditional is used to talk about unreal, hypothetical, or imaginary situations in the present or future. Let us explore its form, uses, and examples in detail.

subsections.subtitle: 4.3.1. Form and Structure
paragraphs: **Type II Conditional** (also called the Second Conditional or Present Unreal Conditional) is used to talk about unreal, hypothetical, or imaginary situations in the present or future. The condition is contrary to fact or unlikely to happen.
**Form:** If + past simple, + would + base verb
**Examples from the module:**
- 'If I met Zinedine Zidane, I would...'
- 'If you helped me look for it instead of telling me what time it was, that would be a big help.'
- 'I'd keep my wallet in the same place every day if I were you.'

**Oxford Reference (Murphy, English Grammar in Use, 4th ed.):** The second conditional is used for hypothetical or unreal situations. The if-clause uses the past simple, and the main clause uses 'would' + base verb. It is used to talk about what would happen if something were true (but it is not).
**Important Note 1:** With the verb 'be', use 'were' for all subjects in the if-clause (especially in formal English).
- Correct: If I were you, I would study harder.
- Informal: If I was you, I would study harder.
**Important Note 2:** Do NOT use 'would' in the if-clause.
- Incorrect: If I would meet him, I would ask him.
- Correct: If I met him, I would ask him.
**Variations:** The main clause can also use 'could' or 'might'.
- If I had more time, I could help you.
- If she studied harder, she might pass.
definitions: A conditional used for unreal, hypothetical, or imaginary situations in the present or future.
Another name for Type II Conditional.
Another name for Type II Conditional.
key_points: Type II: unreal/hypothetical present or future.
Form: If + past simple, + would + base verb.
Use 'were' for all subjects with 'be' (formal).
Do NOT use 'would' in the if-clause.
Main clause can use 'could' or 'might'.
Condition is contrary to fact or unlikely.
formulas: Type II Conditional
If + past simple, + would + base verb
If I met him, I would ask him.
Type II with Were
If + subject + were, + would + base verb
If I were you, I would study.
Type II with Could
If + past simple, + could + base verb
If I had time, I could help.
Type II with Might
If + past simple, + might + base verb
If she studied, she might pass.

subsections.subtitle: 4.3.2. Uses and Examples
paragraphs: **Use 1: Hypothetical situations in the present or future.**
- If I met Zinedine Zidane, I would ask for his autograph.
- If I had a million dollars, I would travel the world.
**Use 2: Giving advice (with 'If I were you').**
- If I were you, I would study harder.
- If I were you, I would apologize.
**Use 3: Imagining impossible or unlikely situations.**
- If I could fly, I would visit every country.
- If she knew the answer, she would tell us.
**More examples:**
- If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
- If we had more time, we could finish the project.
- If he studied more, he might get better grades.
- If it rained, we would stay indoors.
definitions: Imagined or suggested but not necessarily real.
key_points: Type II is used for hypothetical situations.
It can be used for advice with 'If I were you'.
It imagines impossible or unlikely situations.
The if-clause uses past simple.
The main clause uses 'would' + base verb.
Use 'were' for all subjects with 'be' (formal).
tables: If I met him, I would ask him.
If I were you, I would study.
If I could fly, I would travel.

sections.section_introduction: Type III Conditional is used to talk about impossible or unreal situations in the past. Let us explore its form, uses, and examples in detail.

subsections.subtitle: 4.4.1. Form and Structure
paragraphs: **Type III Conditional** (also called the Third Conditional or Past Unreal Conditional) is used to talk about impossible or unreal situations in the past. The condition did not happen, and the result did not happen either. It is often used to express regret or criticism.
**Form:** If + past perfect, + would have + past participle
**Examples from the module:**
- 'If I had met Derartu Tulu immediately after she won the women's 10,000 meters race in the Barcelona Olympics in 1992, I would have...'
- 'I could have got a better mark provided I had worked on the verbs.'
- 'If I had heard you, I would have done it.'

**Oxford Reference (Murphy, English Grammar in Use, 4th ed.):** The third conditional is used for past situations that did not happen. The if-clause uses the past perfect, and the main clause uses 'would have' + past participle. It is used to imagine a different past.
**Important Note:** Do NOT use 'would have' in the if-clause.
- Incorrect: If I would have known, I would have told you.
- Correct: If I had known, I would have told you.
**Variations:** The main clause can also use 'could have' or 'might have'.
- If I had studied harder, I could have passed.
- If she had left earlier, she might have caught the train.
definitions: A conditional used for impossible or unreal situations in the past.
Another name for Type III Conditional.
Another name for Type III Conditional.
key_points: Type III: impossible/unreal past situations.
Form: If + past perfect, + would have + past participle.
Condition did not happen; result did not happen.
Used to express regret or criticism.
Do NOT use 'would have' in the if-clause.
Main clause can use 'could have' or 'might have'.
formulas: Type III Conditional
If + past perfect, + would have + past participle
If I had known, I would have told you.
Type III with Could Have
If + past perfect, + could have + past participle
If I had studied, I could have passed.
Type III with Might Have
If + past perfect, + might have + past participle
If she had left, she might have caught it.
tables: If I had met Derartu Tulu

subsections.subtitle: 4.4.2. Uses and Examples
paragraphs: **Use 1: Expressing regret about the past.**
- If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
- If I had known, I would have told you.
**Use 2: Criticizing past actions.**
- If you had listened to me, you would not have made that mistake.
- If she had been more careful, she would not have lost her keys.
**Use 3: Imagining a different past.**
- If I had met Derartu Tulu, I would have asked for her autograph.
- If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
**More examples:**
- If I had seen him, I would have said hello.
- If they had arrived on time, we would have started together.
- If he had studied medicine, he could have become a doctor.
- If she had taken the job, she might have moved to Addis Ababa.
definitions: A feeling of sadness about something that happened or did not happen.
key_points: Type III is used for impossible past situations.
It expresses regret or criticism.
The if-clause uses past perfect.
The main clause uses 'would have' + past participle.
It imagines a different past.
tables: If I had studied, I would have passed.
If you had listened, you would not have failed.
If I had met her, I would have asked.

paragraphs: The following table summarizes the three main types of conditionals, their forms, and their meanings.

If it rained, I would stay home.

sections.section_introduction: Mixed conditionals combine parts of different conditional types. They are used when the condition and the result refer to different times.

subsections.subtitle: 4.6.1. Form and Structure
paragraphs: **Mixed conditionals** combine parts of different conditional types. They are used when the condition and the result refer to different times.
**Common Mixed Conditional 1: Past condition, present result**
- Form: If + past perfect, + would + base verb
- Example: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. (Condition: past; Result: present)
**Common Mixed Conditional 2: Present condition, past result**
- Form: If + past simple, + would have + past participle
- Example: If I were more careful, I would have caught the mistake. (Condition: present/general; Result: past)

**Oxford Reference (Swan, Practical English Usage, 3rd ed.):** Mixed conditionals are used when the time in the if-clause is different from the time in the main clause. The most common types are past condition with present result, and present condition with past result.
definitions: A conditional that combines parts of different conditional types, with condition and result referring to different times.
key_points: Mixed conditionals combine different types.
Past condition + present result: If + past perfect, would + verb.
Present condition + past result: If + past simple, would have + past participle.
Used when condition and result refer to different times.
formulas: Mixed: Past Condition, Present Result
If + past perfect, + would + base verb
If I had studied, I would be a doctor now.
Mixed: Present Condition, Past Result
If + past simple, + would have + past participle
If I were careful, I would have caught it.
tables: If I had studied, I would be a doctor now.
If I were careful, I would have caught it.

sections.section_title: Other Conditional Words: Unless, Provided, As Long As, In Case
sections.section_introduction: In addition to 'if', English has several other words and phrases that introduce conditions. Let us explore them in detail.

subsections.subtitle: 4.7.1. Form and Uses
paragraphs: **Unless** means 'if not'. It is used in negative conditions.
- Example: Unless you study hard, you will fail. (= If you do not study hard, you will fail.)
**Provided (that) / Providing** means 'on condition that'. It is used for strong conditions.
- Example: You can go out provided that you finish your homework.
**As long as** means 'on condition that' or 'while'.
- Example: You can borrow my car as long as you drive carefully.
**In case** is used to talk about precautions.
- Example: Take an umbrella in case it rains.

**Oxford Reference (Swan, Practical English Usage, 3rd ed.):** These words are used to introduce conditions. 'Unless' means 'except if'. 'Provided/providing that' and 'as long as' mean 'on condition that'. 'In case' is used for precautions.
definitions: A word meaning 'if not'; used in negative conditions.
A phrase meaning 'on condition that' or 'while'.
A phrase used to talk about precautions.
key_points: Unless = if not.
Provided that = on condition that.
As long as = on condition that / while.
In case = as a precaution.
These words introduce conditional clauses.
formulas: Unless
Unless + present simple, + will + base verb
Unless you study, you will fail.
Provided That
Provided that + present simple, + can + base verb
You can go provided that you finish.
As Long As
As long as + present simple, + can + base verb
You can borrow it as long as you drive carefully.
In Case
In case + present simple, + imperative
Take an umbrella in case it rains.
tables: Unless you study, you will fail.
You can go provided that you finish.
You can borrow it as long as you drive carefully.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.

sections.section_introduction: The following are the most common errors students make when using conditional sentences. Study them carefully to avoid them.

subsections.subtitle: 4.8.1. Five Common Errors
paragraphs: **Error 1: Using 'will' in the if-clause of Type I.**
- Incorrect: If you will study, you will pass.
- Correct: If you study, you will pass.
**Error 2: Using 'would' in the if-clause of Type II.**
- Incorrect: If I would meet him, I would ask him.
- Correct: If I met him, I would ask him.
**Error 3: Using 'would have' in the if-clause of Type III.**
- Incorrect: If I would have known, I would have told you.
- Correct: If I had known, I would have told you.
**Error 4: Using 'was' instead of 'were' in Type II (formal).**
- Incorrect (formal): If I was you, I would study harder.
- Correct (formal): If I were you, I would study harder.
**Error 5: Confusing Type II and Type III.**
- Type II: If I had money, I would buy a car. (present unreal)
- Type III: If I had had money, I would have bought a car. (past unreal)
key_points: Never use 'will' in Type I if-clause.
Never use 'would' in Type II if-clause.
Never use 'would have' in Type III if-clause.
Use 'were' for all subjects with 'be' in Type II (formal).
Distinguish Type II (present unreal) from Type III (past unreal).
tables: If you will study, you will pass.
If you study, you will pass.
If I would meet him, I would ask.
If I met him, I would ask.
Would have in Type III if-clause
If I would have known, I would have told you.
If I had known, I would have told you.
If I was you, I would study.
If I were you, I would study.

exercises.question: Circle the correct words in parentheses in Dialogue 1: If I don't finish it tonight, I (get, will get, would get) an F!
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I conditional (real future possibility).
• Explanation & Derivation: The if-clause is present simple ('don't finish'), so the main clause uses 'will' + base verb.
• Final Answer: will get

exercises.question: Dialogue 1: I can help you if you (need, will need, would need) it.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I conditional; if-clause uses present simple.
• Explanation & Derivation: After 'if', use present simple, not 'will' or 'would'.
• Final Answer: need

exercises.question: Dialogue 2: We need to leave right now if we (want, wanted, will want, would want) to get there in time.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I conditional; if-clause uses present simple.
• Explanation & Derivation: The condition is real and possible. Use present simple 'want'.
• Final Answer: want

exercises.question: Dialogue 2: If you helped me look for it instead of telling me what time it was, that (is, was, would be) a big help.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type II conditional (hypothetical present).
• Explanation & Derivation: If-clause uses past simple ('helped'), so main clause uses 'would' + base verb.
• Final Answer: would be

exercises.question: Dialogue 2: I'd keep my wallet in the same place every day if I (am, were, can be) you.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type II conditional with 'be'.
• Explanation & Derivation: In formal English, use 'were' for all subjects with 'be' in the if-clause.
• Final Answer: were

exercises.question: Dialogue 3: I could have got a better mark provided I (worked, work, had worked, have worked) on the verbs.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type III conditional (past unreal).
• Explanation & Derivation: 'Provided' introduces a condition. The main clause uses 'could have got' (past unreal), so the if-clause uses past perfect 'had worked'.
• Final Answer: had worked

exercises.question: Dialogue 3: I (would fail, will fail, would have failed) even if I had studied; that's why I decided not to do it.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type III conditional (past unreal).
• Explanation & Derivation: The if-clause uses past perfect 'had studied', so the main clause uses 'would have' + past participle.
• Final Answer: would have failed

exercises.question: Dialogue 3: Nobody fails an exam as long as they (study, studied, had studied).
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I conditional with 'as long as'.
• Explanation & Derivation: 'As long as' introduces a real condition. Use present simple 'study'.
• Final Answer: study

exercises.question: Dialogue 4: Can I go out on condition that I (did, do, have done, had done) all my homework before leaving.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I conditional with 'on condition that'.
• Explanation & Derivation: 'On condition that' introduces a real condition. Use present simple 'do'.
• Final Answer: do

exercises.question: Dialogue 4: If you (do, did, had done, have done) your homework when I asked you, you would be allowed to go out now.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Mixed conditional (past condition, present result).
• Explanation & Derivation: The main clause uses 'would be' (present result), so the if-clause uses past perfect 'had done' (past condition).
• Final Answer: had done

exercises.question: Dialogue 4: If I had heard you, I (would have done, will do, would do, will have done) it.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type III conditional (past unreal).
• Explanation & Derivation: The if-clause uses past perfect 'had heard', so the main clause uses 'would have' + past participle.
• Final Answer: would have done

exercises.question: Dialogue 4: It (won't, wouldn't, wouldn't have) hurt if you listened to me once in a while.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type II conditional (hypothetical present).
• Explanation & Derivation: The if-clause uses past simple 'listened', so the main clause uses 'would not' (wouldn't) + base verb.
• Final Answer: wouldn't

exercises.question: Dialogue 4: If you (did, do, had done, have done) it more often, your life would be much easier.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type II conditional (hypothetical present).
• Explanation & Derivation: The main clause uses 'would be', so the if-clause uses past simple 'did'.
• Final Answer: did

exercises.question: What would you do if you were the mother? Write your answer and show it to a partner.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type II conditional (hypothetical present) for advice.
• Explanation & Derivation: Use 'If I were the mother, I would...' + base verb.
• Final Answer: If I were the mother, I would listen to my child first and then explain why homework must be done before going out. I would also set clear rules and consequences.

exercises.question: Write as many conditional sentences as you can based on the information in the table about National Parks in Ethiopia. Example: If tourists go to the Kafta Sheraro National Park, they will see the African elephant.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I conditional for real possibilities.
• Explanation & Derivation: Use 'If tourists go to [park], they will see [animal].' Use present simple in if-clause and 'will' + base verb in main clause.
• Final Answer:
  - If tourists go to the Kafta Sheraro National Park, they will see the African elephant.
  - If tourists go to the Kafta Sheraro National Park, they will see the ground squirrel.
  - If tourists go to the Kafta Sheraro National Park, they will see the crested porcupine.
  - If tourists go to the Simien Mountains National Park, they will see the Walia ibex.
  - If tourists go to the Simien Mountains National Park, they will see the Gelada baboon.
  - If tourists go to the Simien Mountains National Park, they will see the caracal.
  - If tourists go to the Bale Mountains National Park, they will see the Mountain Nyala.
  - If tourists go to the Bale Mountains National Park, they will see the Ethiopian wolf.
  - If tourists go to the Bale Mountains National Park, they will see the spotted hyena.
  - If tourists go to the Nechisar National Park, they will see the plains zebra.
  - If tourists go to the Nechisar National Park, they will see the greater kudu.
  - If tourists go to the Nechisar National Park, they will see the dik-dik.
  - If tourists go to the Yangudi Rassa National Park, they will see the Beisa oryx.
  - If tourists go to the Yangudi Rassa National Park, they will see the Abyssinian mahr.
  - If tourists go to the Yangudi Rassa National Park, they will see the Grevy's zebra.

exercises.question: Complete the following table with your own example sentences for each conditional type.
exercises.answer:
DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION:
• Given & Concept: Type I, II, III conditionals.
• Explanation & Derivation:
  - Type I: If + present simple, will + base verb.
  - Type II: If + past simple, would + base verb.
  - Type III: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.
• Final Answer:
  - Type I: If I study hard, I will pass the exam.
  - Type II: If I studied hard, I would pass the exam.
  - Type III: If I had studied hard, I would have passed the exam.

summary:
CHAPTER SUMMARY — CHAPTER 4: CONDITIONALS (University Freshman Communicative English Language Skills I):
This chapter covers conditionals in full detail: (1) What is a conditional sentence — if-clause + main clause; (2) Type I Conditional (First/Future Real) — If + present simple, will + base verb — for real/possible future situations; (3) Type II Conditional (Second/Present Unreal) — If + past simple, would + base verb — for unreal/hypothetical present or future; (4) Type III Conditional (Third/Past Unreal) — If + past perfect, would have + past participle — for impossible/unreal past; (5) Comparison of the three conditionals; (6) Mixed conditionals (past condition/present result and present condition/past result); (7) Other conditional words (unless, provided that, as long as, in case); and (8) Common errors with conditionals. The document provides expanded explanations from Oxford grammar references (Murphy, Swan), formal definitions, key takeaway points, structured comparison tables, visual diagrams, and step-by-step exercise solutions. © Acadia.
